title: Monomorphization Binary Bloat
pattern: Writing large, non-performance-critical functions that accept highly generic arguments, causing the compiler to duplicate the entire function's machine code for every unique type combination passed.
why_bad: Results in static compilation binary bloat. The compiler generates multiple identical copies of heavy formatting and file I/O logic in the final binary (one for `String`, one for `&str`, one for `u32`, etc.), inflating the binary size and severely degrading instruction cache performance.
detection: Identify large functions (50+ lines) containing complex, non-trivial logic that accept generic parameters with broad bounds, particularly when they are called with many different concrete types.
counterexample: Performance-critical, hot-loop functions (like matrix multiplication or sorting algorithms) where monomorphization and compiler inlining are vital for raw execution speed.
fix: Apply the "inner-function pattern" or "type-erasure". Extract the non-generic core of the function into a private, helper function that works on concrete references (like `&str` or `&dyn Display`).
source: *Richard L. Sites - Understanding Software Dynamics (2021)*, Chapter 9, "Aggregate Measures" (Code Cache Performance); *Jon Gjengset - Rust for Rustaceans (2021)*, Chapter 2.
